query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Enhanced short-range ordering (SRO) between aluminum (Al) and nickel (Ni) promotes the formation of partial B2 ordering, which in turn stabilizes the bcc phase relative to the fcc phase in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys. This mechanism governs phase stability and is key to retaining a desirable combination of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy produced with a mixed fcc and bcc microstructure via casting or solution annealing.
generation.intervention: Apply different heat treatment protocols (e.g., varying quench rates and aging times) to systematically tailor the degree of Al–Ni short-range ordering without altering the overall composition.
generation.conditions: Identical alloy compositions exposed to controlled heat treatments, followed by testing across a temperature range from cryogenic (<77 K) to high-temperature (>800 °C) environments as well as under corrosive and radiation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial B2 ordering domains arising from enhanced Al–Ni short-range ordering.
generation.mechanism: Tailored heat treatments promote localized Al–Ni SRO, which reduces the free energy of the bcc phase through B2-like ordering. This thermodynamic stabilization shifts the phase equilibrium in favor of bcc (or mixed bcc-fcc states that incorporate B2 domains), thereby enhancing the alloy's mechanical and environmental performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with increased Al–Ni short-range order will exhibit an increased fraction or stabilization of the bcc (B2) phase, leading to enhanced high-temperature strength, improved radiation and corrosion resistance, and maintained or improved toughness at cryogenic temperatures compared to a conventionally heat-treated baseline.
generation.baseline: A control sample subjected to standard heat treatment conditions that results in a balanced fcc/bcc microstructure with minimal targeted enhancement of Al–Ni SRO.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys processed under controlled heat treatment conditions and may not extend to compositions with significantly different elemental ratios or those processed under extreme conditions that introduce additional phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports the linkage between phase engineering and enhanced properties, the precise quantitative impact of Al–Ni SRO on phase stability and mechanical performance relative to other contributing factors (e.g., atomic size mismatch or electronic effects) remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples with identical compositions. Subject each set to different heat treatments designed to vary the degree of Al–Ni SRO (e.g., rapid quenching versus prolonged aging). Characterize the microstructure via synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), diffuse scattering, and atom probe tomography to quantify the bcc phase and B2 ordering. Additionally, perform mechanical tests over high and cryogenic temperature ranges, as well as corrosion and radiation exposure tests.
measurements: Synchrotron XRD for phase fraction analysis
Diffuse scattering and atom probe tomography for detecting partial B2 ordering and SRO
Mechanical tests (tensile, hardness) at high and cryogenic temperatures
Corrosion resistance and radiation tolerance measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with enhanced Al–Ni SRO (as measured by increased B2 ordering) do not exhibit a statistically significant shift toward a greater bcc phase fraction or improved high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis that Al–Ni SRO is the mechanistic driver of phase stability in this system would be falsified.

Producing HEAs with a balanced combination of properties needed for practical applications still remains a significant challenge, however. It has very high ductility (70–80%) at both room and cryogenic temperatures, and record breaking fracture toughness under cryogenic conditions [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are composed of 5–35 at% of five or more elements, have high configurational entropy, do not form intermetallic compounds, and have a single-phase face-centered cubic structure or body-centered cubic structure. In particular, refractory HEAs (RHEAs), based on refractory materials with excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, have high strength and hardness at room temperature and excellent mechanical properties at low and high temperatures. In this study, the Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al RHEAs were deposited using direct energy deposition (DED). In the microstructure of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, the sigma, BCC A2, and Ti2Ni phases appeared to be different from the BCC A2, BCC B2, and Laves phases predicted in the phase diagram. This microstructure was similar to that of the casted Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al and had a constructed fine grain size. It was found that the growth of these microstructures was due to the DED process, which has a fast solidification rate. The fine grain size caused high hardness, and the microhardness of the Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al was measured to be about 900 HV. RHEAs have a crystal structure such as FCC, FCC+BCC, and BCC phases, a microstructure including a precipitated phase, and intermetallic compounds such as the BCC B2 phase and Laves phase []. Most research using HEAs was conducted during evaluation of the basic properties by manufacturing ingots using arc melting and casting []. The conventional casting method of manufacturing HEAs has the problem of difficulty in forming a single-phase solid solution due to a low cooling rate. As the size of the manufactured HEA increases, it is difficult to secure the uniformity of the microstructure because the internal cooling rate and the external cooling rate are different. The non-uniformed microstructure causes degradation and non-uniformity of the mechanical properties of the HEAs [,]. decision.trend: Early work on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni eutectic alloys (PMC6353877::webcard) showed that combining an ultrafine-grained lamellar microstructure with hierarchical phase separation can achieve exceptional strength–ductility synergy. Concurrently, research on transformation-induced plasticity in related Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–based alloys (PMC6393512::webcard) used thermodynamic tuning of fcc–bcc phase stability to enhance mechanical properties. Although these studies demonstrated that phase engineering greatly influences performance, they did not fully resolve which specific atomic-scale interactions ultimately fix metastable phase boundaries across wide temperature and environmental conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether short-range ordering (SRO) among Al, Ni, and other elements, localized electronic effects, or atomic-size mismatches primarily dictate fcc/bcc balance in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni. Understanding which factor governs that balance—and how it promotes the remarkable combination of high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and ductility at cryogenic temperatures—requires isolating the underlying driving force for phase stability.
decision.lever: Tailor Al–Ni short-range ordering via different heat treatments (e.g., varying quench rates or aging times) and measure the emergence of partial B2 ordering and bcc-fcc partitioning using diffuse scattering, synchrotron XRD, and atom probe tomography under identical composition conditions.
decision.why: By systematically tuning the degree of Al–Ni short-range order without changing composition, one can directly test whether such ordering triggers or stabilizes the bcc phase and influences mechanical properties. If enhanced B2-like domains correlate with improved mechanical property retention at both high and cryogenic temperatures, that supports an SRO-driven stability mechanism. Lack of the predicted bcc or B2-related features or the absence of corresponding mechanical benefits would falsify this hypothesis.
